danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Pierre havde i den sidste tid sjældent set sin kone alene. Både i Petersborg og i Moskva var deres hus altid fuldt af gæster. Natten efter duellen gik han ikke ind i sit soveværelse, men blev, som han ofte gjorde, i sin fars værelse — det enorme rum, hvor grev Bezukhov var død.

Han lagde sig på sofaen for at falde i søvn og glemme alt, hvad der var sket, men kunne det ikke. En sådan storm af følelser, tanker og minder rejste sig pludselig i ham, at han hverken kunne falde i søvn eller forblive på ét sted, men måtte springe op og vandre rastløst rundt. Nu syntes han at se hende i de første dage af deres ægteskab med bare skuldre og et sløret, lidenskabeligt blik, og umiddelbart efter så han Dolokhov's smukke, frække, hårde og spottende ansigt, som han havde set det ved banketten, og derefter det samme ansigt — blegt, dirrende og lidende — som det havde set ud, da han tumlede og sank ned i sneen.

»Hvad er der sket?« spurgte han sig selv. »Jeg har dræbt hendes elsker, ja, dræbt min kones elsker. Ja, det var det. Og hvorfor? Hvordan kom jeg til det?« — »Fordi du giftede dig med hende,« svarede en indre stemme.

»Men hvori bestod min skyld?« spurgte han. »I at gifte mig med hende uden at elske hende; i at bedrage mig selv og hende.« Og han huskede tydeligt det øjeblik efter souper hos fyrst Vasilij, da han sagde de ord, han havde fundet så vanskelige at udtale: »Jeg elsker Dem.« »Det hele stammer fra det! Allerede dengang følte jeg det,« tænkte han. »Jeg følte dengang, at det ikke var rigtigt, at jeg ikke havde ret til at gøre det. Og sådan er det gået.«

Han huskede sin bryllupsrejse og rødmede ved erindringen. Særligt levende, ydmygende og pinefuldt var mindet om, hvordan han en dag kort efter brylluppet var kommet ud af soveværelset i sin silkeslobrok lidt før middag og i sit arbejdsværelse havde fundet sin godsforvalter, der ærbødigt bøjede sig, kiggede på hans ansigt og hans slobrok og smilede let, som for at udtrykke respektfuld forståelse for sin herres lykke.

»Men hvor ofte har jeg ikke været stolt af hende — stolt af hendes majestætiske skønhed og selskabelige takt,« tænkte han; »stolt af mit hus, hvori hun modtog hele Petersborg, stolt af hendes utilnærmelighed og skønhed. Og det var altså dét, jeg var stolt af! Dengang troede jeg, at jeg ikke forstod hende. Hvor ofte har jeg ikke, når jeg grublede over hendes karakter, sagt til mig selv, at det var mig, der var skyld i, at jeg ikke forstod hende, ikke forstod den vedvarende ro og selvtilfredshed og manglen på alle interesser og ønsker — og hele hemmeligheden ligger i den forfærdelige sandhed, at hun er en fordærvet kvinde. Nu, da jeg har sagt det forfærdelige ord til mig selv, er alt blevet klart.«

»Anatole plejede at komme og låne penge af hende og kyssede hendes bare skuldre. Hun gav ham ikke pengene, men lod sig kysse. Hendes far forsøgte for sjov at vække hendes jalousi, og hun svarede med et roligt smil, at hun ikke var dum nok til at være jaloux: 'Lad ham gøre, som han vil,' sagde hun om mig. En dag spurgte jeg hende, om hun mærkede tegn på graviditet. Hun lo hånligt og sagde, at hun ikke var dum nok til at ønske sig børn, og at hun ikke havde tænkt sig at få børn med mig.«
Så huskede han grovheden og plumpheden i hendes tankegang og vulgariteten i de udtryk, der faldt hende naturligt, skønt hun var opvokset i de mest aristokratiske kredse.

»Jeg er ikke noget fjols ... Prøv bare ... Allez-vous promener,« * plejede hun at sige. Ofte, når Pierre så den succes, hun havde hos unge og gamle, mænd som kvinder, kunne han ikke forstå, hvorfor han ikke elskede hende.
* »Forsvind herfra.«

»Ja, jeg har aldrig elsket hende,« sagde han til sig selv; »jeg vidste, hun var en fordærvet kvinde,« gentog han, »men turde ikke indrømme det over for mig selv. Og nu sidder Dolokhov i sneen med et tvungent smil og dør måske, mens han møder min anger med en slags tvungen tapperhed!«
Pierre var et af de mennesker, der trods ydre tegn på såkaldt svag karakter ikke søger en fortrolig i deres trængsler. Han fordøjede sine lidelser alene.

»Det er alt, alt hendes skyld,« sagde han til sig selv; »men hvad så? Hvorfor bandt jeg mig til hende? Hvorfor sagde jeg 'Je vous aime' *, hvilket var løgn og værre end løgn? Jeg er skyldig og må udholde ... hvad? En plet på mit navn? En ulykke for livet? Åh, det er meningsløst,« tænkte han. »Pletten på mit navn og min ære — det har intet med mig selv at gøre.«
* Jeg elsker Dem.

»Ludvig den Sekstende blev henrettet, fordi de sagde, han var vanæret og en forbryder,« passerede gennem Pierres tanker, »og fra deres synspunkt havde de ret, ligesom dem, der kanoniserede ham og døde en martyrdød for hans skyld. Så blev Robespierre halshugget, fordi han var en despot. Hvem har ret, og hvem har uret? Ingen! Men hvis du lever — så lev: i morgen dør du, som jeg kunne have gjort det for en time siden. Og er det umagen værd at pine sig selv, når man kun har et øjeblik af liv sammenlignet med evigheden?«

Men i det øjeblik, han forestillede sig beroliget af sådanne refleksioner, stod hun pludselig for ham, som hun var i de øjeblikke, hvor han stærkest havde udtrykt sin uoprigtige kærlighed til hende, og han følte blodet strømme til hjertet og måtte igen rejse sig og gå omkring og bryde og rive i alt, hvad der kom ham for hånden. »Hvorfor sagde jeg 'Je vous aime'?« gentog han ustandseligt. Og da han havde sagt det for tiende gang, faldt Molières ord ham ind: »Mais que diable allait-il faire dans cette galère?« * og han begyndte at le af sig selv.
* »Men hvad fanden lavede han i den galej?«

Om natten kaldte han sin kammertjener og bad ham pakke til Petersborg. Han kunne ikke forestille sig at tale med hende nu. Han besluttede at rejse næste dag og efterlade et brev, hvori han meddelte sin hensigt om for altid at skille sig fra hende.
Næste morgen, da kammertjeneren kom ind med kaffen, lå Pierre og sov på ottomanen med en åben bog i hånden.
Han vågnede og så sig forvirret omkring et øjeblik, ude af stand til at fatte, hvor han var.
»Grevinden har bedt mig forhøre, om Deres excellence er hjemme,« sagde kammertjeneren.

Men før Pierre kunne beslutte, hvad han ville svare, trådte grevinden selv ind i rummet i en hvid atlaskesslobrok broderet med sølv og med sit hår sat enkelt op (to vældige fletninger to gange rundt om hendes smukke hoved som en krone), rolig og majestætisk, bortset fra en vred rynke på sin noget fremtrædende marmorpande. Med sin urokkelige ro begyndte hun ikke at tale i tjenernes nærvær. Hun vidste om duellen og var kommet for at tale om den. Hun ventede, til kammertjeneren havde sat kaffestellet og var gået ud. Pierre så sky på hende over sine briller, og som en hare, der omringet af hunde lægger ørerne tilbage og fortsat ligger ubevægeligt sammenpresset foran sine fjender, forsøgte han at fortsætte med at læse. Men han følte, at det var meningsløst og umuligt, og sendte endnu et sky blik mod hende. Hun satte sig ikke ned, men så på ham med et foragteligt smil og ventede, til tjeneren var gået.
»Nå, hvad er det nu? Hvad har du nu lavet, vil jeg gerne vide?« sagde hun strengt.
»Jeg? Hvad har jeg ...?« stammede Pierre.
»Se mig an — en helt, hva? Nå, hvad handlede den duel om? Hvad skulle det bevise? Hvad? Jeg spørger dig.«
Pierre vendte sig tungt om på ottomanen og åbnede munden, men kunne ikke svare.

»Hvis du ikke vil svare, skal jeg nok sige dig det ...« Helene fortsatte. »Du tror på alt, hvad man fortæller dig. Man har fortalt dig ...« Helene lo, »at Dolokhov var min elsker,« sagde hun på fransk med sin grove ligefremhed og brugte ordet amant lige så afslappet som ethvert andet ord, »og du troede det! Nå, hvad har du bevist? Hvad beviser den duel? At du er en tåbe, que vous êtes un sot — men det vidste alle i forvejen. Hvad bliver resultatet? At jeg bliver hele Moskvas grin, at alle vil sige, at du, beruset og uden at vide, hvad du lavede, udfordrede en mand, du er jaloux på uden grund.« Helene hævede stemmen og blev mere og mere ophidset. »En mand, der er bedre end du på alle måder ...«
»Hm ... hm ...!« gryntede Pierre og rynkede panden uden at se på hende og uden at røre en muskel.
»Og hvordan kunne du tro, han var min elsker? Hvorfor? Fordi jeg kan lide hans selskab? Hvis du var klogere og mere elskværdig, ville jeg foretrække dit.«
»Tal ikke til mig ... det beder jeg om,« mumlede Pierre hæst.

»Hvorfor skulle jeg ikke tale? Jeg kan tale, som jeg vil, og jeg siger dig ligeud, at der ikke er mange koner med ægtemænd som dig, der ikke ville have taget sig elskere, men det har jeg ikke gjort,« sagde hun.

Pierre ville sige noget, så på hende med øjne, hvis mærkelige udtryk hun ikke forstod, og lagde sig ned igen. Han led fysisk i det øjeblik, der var en vægt på hans bryst, og han kunne ikke ånde. Han vidste, at han måtte gøre noget for at afslutte denne lidelse, men det, han ønskede at gøre, var for frygteligt.
»Vi må hellere gå fra hinanden,« mumlede han med brudt stemme.
»Gå fra hinanden? Gerne, men kun hvis du giver mig en formue,« sagde Helene. »Gå fra hinanden! Det kan du tro, du skræmmer mig med!«
Pierre sprang op fra sofaen og styrtede vaklende hen mod hende.
»Jeg slår dig ihjel!« råbte han og greb marmorpladen af bordet med en kraft, han aldrig før havde følt, og tog et skridt mod hende med den løftede plade.

Helenes ansigt blev forfærdeligt, hun skreg og sprang til side. Faderens natur viste sig i Pierre. Han mærkede fascinationen og glæden ved vanviddet. Han slyngede pladen ned, knuste den, og med udstrakte hænder styrtede han mod hende og råbte: »Ud!« med en så forfærdelig stemme, at hele huset hørte det med gru. Gud ved, hvad han ville have gjort i det øjeblik, hvis Helene ikke var flygtet fra rummet.
En uge senere gav Pierre sin kone fuld rådighed over alle sine godser i Storrusland, der udgjorde størstedelen af hans formue, og rejste alene til Petersborg.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Pierre had rarely seen his wife alone lately. Both in Petersburg and in Moscow their house was always full of guests. The night after the duel he didn't go to his bedroom but instead, as he often did, stayed in his father's room — that enormous room where Count Bezukhov had died.

He lay down on the sofa intending to fall asleep and forget everything that had happened, but he couldn't. Such a storm of feelings, thoughts, and memories suddenly overwhelmed him that he couldn't sleep or even stay in one place. He had to jump up and pace the room with rapid steps. One moment he seemed to see her in the early days of their marriage, with bare shoulders and a languid, passionate expression on her face, and then immediately he saw beside her Dolokhov's handsome, insolent, hard, and mocking face as it had been at the banquet — and then that same face, pale, trembling, and suffering, as it had looked when he staggered and sank into the snow.

"What has happened?" he asked himself. "I've killed her lover — yes, killed my wife's lover. Yes, that's what happened! And why? How did I come to do it?" — "Because you married her," answered an inner voice.

"But how was I to blame?" he asked. "For marrying her without loving her; for deceiving yourself and her." And he vividly recalled that moment after supper at Prince Vasili's when he had spoken those words he found so hard to say: "I love you." "It all comes from that! Even then I felt it," he thought. "I felt then that it wasn't right, that I had no right to do it. And so it has turned out."

He remembered his honeymoon and blushed at the memory. One recollection was particularly vivid, humiliating, and shameful — how one day, shortly after his marriage, he had come out of the bedroom into his study a little before noon in his silk dressing gown, and found his head steward there. The man bowed respectfully, glanced at his face and his dressing gown, and smiled slightly, as if expressing a tactful understanding of his master's happiness.

"But how often I was proud of her — proud of her majestic beauty and social skill," he thought. "I was proud of my house, where she entertained all of Petersburg, proud of her cool composure and beauty. So this is what I was proud of! Back then I thought I didn't understand her. How often, when thinking about her character, I told myself that I was the one at fault for not understanding her, for not understanding that constant poise and self-satisfaction and complete lack of interests or desires. And the whole secret lies in the terrible truth that she is a corrupt woman. Now I've said that terrible word to myself, everything has become clear."

"Anatole used to come to borrow money from her and would kiss her bare shoulders. She didn't give him the money but let herself be kissed. Her father once tried, as a joke, to make her jealous, and she replied with a calm smile that she wasn't stupid enough to be jealous. 'Let him do what he wants,' she used to say about me. One day I asked her if she had any signs of pregnancy. She laughed scornfully and said she wasn't fool enough to want children, and that she wasn't going to have any children by me."
Then he recalled the coarseness and bluntness of her thoughts and the vulgarity of her expressions, despite her aristocratic upbringing.
"'I'm not that stupid.... Just you try.... Get lost,' she used to say. Seeing how successful she was with young and old men and women, Pierre often couldn't understand why he didn't love her.
* "Get lost."

"Yes, I never loved her," he said to himself. "I knew she was a corrupt woman," he repeated, "but I didn't dare admit it to myself. And now Dolokhov is sitting in the snow with a forced smile, perhaps dying, while I face my remorse with some kind of forced bravado!"
Pierre was one of those people who, despite appearing to have what's called a weak character, don't seek a confidant when they're in trouble. He processed his suffering alone.

"It's all her fault," he told himself. "But what does that matter? Why did I tie myself to her? Why did I say 'I love you' to her — which was a lie, and worse than a lie? I'm guilty and must endure... what? A stain on my name? A lifelong misfortune? Oh, that's nonsense," he thought. "A stain on my name and honor — that's something separate from who I really am."
* I love you.

"Louis XVI was executed because they said he was dishonorable and a criminal," the thought came to Pierre. "And from their point of view, they were right — just as those were right who made him a saint and died as martyrs for his sake. Then Robespierre was beheaded for being a tyrant. Who is right and who is wrong? No one! But if you're alive — live. Tomorrow you'll die, just as I might have died an hour ago. And is it worth tormenting yourself when you have only a moment of life compared to eternity?"

But the moment he imagined himself calmed by such thoughts, she suddenly came into his mind as she had been in those moments when he'd most strongly expressed his fake love for her, and he felt the blood rush to his heart and had to get up again and move around and smash and tear at whatever came to hand. "Why did I tell her 'I love you'?" he kept repeating to himself. And after saying it for the tenth time, Moliere's words came to him: "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?" — and he began to laugh at himself.
* "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?"

During the night he called his valet and told him to pack for Petersburg. He couldn't imagine how he could face her now. He decided to leave the next day and write her a letter informing her of his intention to separate from her forever.
The next morning, when the valet came in with coffee, Pierre was lying asleep on the ottoman with an open book in his hand.
He woke up and looked around for a while with a startled expression, unable to grasp where he was.
"The countess asked me to inquire whether your excellency was at home," said the valet.

But before Pierre could decide what answer to send, the countess herself entered the room. She wore a white satin dressing gown embroidered with silver, her hair simply arranged — two thick braids wound twice around her lovely head like a crown. She was calm and majestic, except for an angry crease on her rather prominent marble forehead. With unshakable composure she didn't speak in front of the valet. She knew about the duel and had come to discuss it. She waited until the valet had set down the coffee things and left. Pierre looked at her timidly over his spectacles, like a hare that, surrounded by hounds, flattens its ears and crouches motionless before its enemies — he tried to go on reading. But realizing this was pointless and impossible, he glanced at her timidly again. She didn't sit down but stood looking at him with a contemptuous smile, waiting for the valet to leave.
"Well, what's this about? What have you been up to now, I'd like to know?" she asked sternly.
"Me? What have I...?" Pierre stammered.
"So you're a hero now, are you? Come on, what was this duel about? What is it supposed to prove? What? I'm asking you."
Pierre rolled over heavily on the ottoman and opened his mouth but couldn't reply.

"If you won't answer, I'll tell you myself..." Helene continued. "You believe everything people tell you. You were told" — Helene laughed — "that Dolokhov was my lover," she said with her characteristic blunt directness, tossing out the word as casually as any other, "and you believed it! Well, what have you proved? What does this duel prove? That you're a fool — but everybody already knew that. What's going to happen now? I'll be the laughingstock of all Moscow. Everyone will say that you, drunk and clueless about what you were doing, challenged a man you were jealous of for no reason." Helene's voice rose and she grew more and more agitated. "A man who is better than you in every way..."
"Hmm... hmm..." Pierre growled, frowning without looking at her and not moving a muscle.
"And how could you believe he was my lover? Why? Because I enjoy his company? If you were more intelligent and more pleasant, I'd prefer yours."
"Don't talk to me... please," Pierre muttered hoarsely.
"Why shouldn't I talk? I can say whatever I want, and I'll tell you plainly that very few wives with husbands like you would have avoided taking lovers — but I haven't done that," she said.

Pierre wanted to say something. He looked at her with a strange expression she didn't understand, then lay down again. He was in physical agony at that moment — there was a weight on his chest and he couldn't breathe. He knew he had to do something to end this suffering, but what he wanted to do was too terrible.
"We should separate," he muttered in a broken voice.
"Separate? Fine, but only if you give me a fortune," said Helene. "Separate! As if that's supposed to scare me!"
Pierre leaped up from the sofa and rushed staggering toward her.
"I'll kill you!" he shouted, and seizing the marble top of a table with a strength he'd never felt before, he took a step toward her, brandishing the heavy slab.

Helene's face became terrified. She shrieked and sprang aside. His father's nature showed itself in Pierre. He felt the thrill and ecstasy of rage. He hurled down the marble slab, shattering it, and lunging toward her with outstretched hands, he roared "Get out!" in such a terrible voice that the whole house heard it with horror. God knows what he would have done if Helene hadn't fled the room.
A week later Pierre gave his wife full control over all his estates in central Russia, which made up the greater part of his wealth, and left for Petersburg alone.
